title: sleep
hook: deep sleep leaves nothing to tell at breakfast; the Brihadaranyaka describes it anyway, with a falcon

segments.voice: Yesterday, sleep and the dream: the dreamer self-lit, making chariots and rivers where there are none.

Deep sleep is the one part of the night with nothing to report. No dream to tell over breakfast. Just a gap, and then the alarm. A gap seems an odd thing to teach. The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad tries anyway. Yajnavalkya, still talking with King Janaka, has walked through waking and through dreams. Now he goes one step further down, and to describe it, he reaches for a bird. Today, the sleep with no dreams in it.
screen: `NOTHING TO REPORT.` → `A GAP, THEN THE ALARM.` → `ONE STEP FURTHER DOWN.`

segments.voice: Here's the bird, paraphrased. A falcon, or an eagle, has been flying in the open sky. It's tired, so it folds its wings and drops to its nest. In the same way, a person hurries toward that state where, asleep, he wants nothing at all and sees no dream. Then Yajnavalkya says something stranger. There, a father is not a father, a mother is not a mother. The worlds are not worlds, the gods not gods, the Vedas not Vedas. A thief is not a thief. He is untouched by good and untouched by evil, the text says, for he has crossed over all the sorrows of the heart. Three things. First, the folded wings. The falcon isn't defeated. It flew all day; folding the wings is just the other half of flying. Second, the roles. Every name a person carries by day, parent, worker, friend, the one with a reputation, even the one with a past, is set down in deep sleep. Not erased. Set down. In the morning they're picked back up. Third, the sorrows of the heart. The text doesn't say grief is cured. It says only that, in that state, the sleeper has crossed over it: a nightly crossing, made without effort. And for honesty: Yajnavalkya isn't saying the goal of life is to sleep well. Deep sleep, for him, is a clue, a nightly taste of being without wanting. The Mandukya Upanishad lines up waking, dreaming and deep sleep, and points past all of them.
screen: `THE FALCON FOLDS ITS WINGS` · `A FATHER IS NOT A FATHER` · `THE SORROWS OF THE HEART, CROSSED` · `A CLUE, NOT THE GOAL`

segments.voice: Name, silently, one role you carried today, parent, worker, friend, student, the one who has to answer, and with the next breath out set it down beside you, not thrown away, just put down. Then the next, and when there are no more names, rest in whatever is left. If you pray, rest in prayer there.
Sleep. In deep sleep, the Brihadaranyaka says, a person wants nothing, sees no dream, and has crossed the sorrows of the heart, like a falcon folding its wings. Today's word.
Your line: sleep. Every name is set down for the night, and picked up again in the morning. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Vedanta teachers study deep, dreamless sleep, sushupti, beside waking and dreaming, and read Yajnavalkya's falcon as a picture of the self at rest.

original.note: Sanskrit sushupti: deep, dreamless sleep, the name later Vedanta teachers give the state this passage describes.

chat.says: Why would an Upanishad bother describing dreamless sleep? Nothing happens in it.
options: Yajnavalkya sees a clue there: wanting nothing, every role set down, the heart's sorrows crossed.
Yajnavalkya calls it the goal of life, so the wise try to sleep as much as they can.
Yajnavalkya says the sleeper's roles are erased for good, so you wake a new person.
chat.meaning: In the Brihadaranyaka, deep sleep is a clue, not the goal: like a tired falcon folding its wings, the sleeper wants nothing, and every role is set down.

notes: Brihadaranyaka 4.3.19: confirm the falcon (shyena) or eagle (suparna) paraphrase and 'na kanchana kamam kamayate na kanchana svapnam pashyati'.
4.3.22: confirm the list as paraphrased and 'crossed all the sorrows of the heart' (tirno hi tada sarvan chokan hridayasya bhavati).
Editor pass: removed the unsourced generalization about what grieving people report; 'later teachers' now names the cited Mandukya; the hook no longer tells the listener what they'd think.
'A few clear seconds before remembering a loss' is an everyday picture, not a claim from the text; phrased as 'people who are grieving sometimes speak of', not as the listener's experience.
'Later teachers lined up waking, dreaming and deep sleep and pointed past them' refers to the Mandukya's turiya; kept without counts.
Sushupti is a later technical term; the note says so.
